name: Spaces
baseline: jemalloc (also snmalloc, tcmalloc, Hoard in the same table)
workload: mimalloc-bench workloads (larson, malloc-large, mleak, glibc-simple, xmalloc-test, mstress, spacesbench, glibc-thread) built against libspaces.a; median of 3 runs
claimed_speedup: larson 124 M ops/s, ranked #2 and ahead of jemalloc, snmalloc, tcmalloc and Hoard; malloc-large 6.0 ms/alloc #2 (beats jemalloc, snmalloc, Hoard); mleak 0.26 s #2; glibc-simple 6.9 s #3 (beats jemalloc, snmalloc); top 3 on 7 of 8 workloads, #6 on glibc-thread
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -pthread -fPIC for the allocator; flags of the baseline allocators and mimalloc-bench builds not stated
tradeoffs: x86-64 Linux only in the single-file build; 8-byte minimum allocation; 64 KB virtual footprint per slab; every free() reads the slab header (one possible L1 miss); explicit heap regions, budgets, heap walking and shared-memory heaps in addition to malloc replacement; weak on heavy thread churn (500 threads).
caveats: First-party table gives ranks and absolute numbers for Spaces only, not the competitors' numbers; CPU model, core count, kernel and compiler version are not stated; the repo has only 2 commits (Mar 2026). Reproducible via bench.sh using mimalloc-bench, but the hardware gap keeps it at C. Loses on glibc-thread (#6).
found_via: Hacker News: Show HN thread 'A single-file C allocator with explicit heaps and tuning knobs' (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47520807), seen via WebSearch snippets only

name: SGCL
baseline: malloc via std::unique_ptr / std::shared_ptr (macOS libmalloc nano zone); also Go and Java ZGC collectors
workload: Per-object allocation cost in ns for 32 B and 256 B objects on 1, 4 and 24 threads, plus binary-trees and a shared-graph workload, compared with unique_ptr, shared_ptr, Go and Java ZGC
claimed_speedup: 32 B allocation 2.8 ns on 1 thread vs unique_ptr 17.1 ns and shared_ptr 16.3 ns (about 6x, derived from page data); 32 B on 4 threads 3.5 vs 17.4 and 16.5 ns; 32 B on 24 threads 11.7 vs 23.2 and 22.6 ns; 256 B on 24 threads is slower than malloc: 71.4 vs 23.5 ns
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG; Go 1.27.1 GOGC=100; OpenJDK 26.0.2 generational ZGC
hardware: Mac Studio Apple M2 Ultra (16 performance + 8 efficiency cores), 64 GB, macOS 26.5
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 concurrent non-moving generational mark-and-sweep GC with its own managed pointer types (tracked_ptr etc.), containers and 15 library modules; programs must adopt sgcl pointer types; conservative stack scanning; tested on Apple Silicon only (Linux and Windows pending).
caveats: The docs deliberately leave Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC out of the tables, so there is no head-to-head with Boehm GC; the malloc baseline is macOS nano malloc, not glibc, jemalloc or mimalloc; Go and Java columns were run on 19 Sep 2026 at -O2 C++ build while C++ columns on 4 Oct 2026; no number reproduced on x86-64 or Linux yet; slower than malloc for 256 B objects at 24 threads.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch for concurrent GC library C++ pauseless surfaced the HN thread 'High-performance garbage collection for C++' (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49695331) and the sgcl repo

name: Mesh
baseline: jemalloc (Firefox and Redis) and glibc malloc (SPEC CPU2006, Ruby)
workload: Peak or mean heap size of Firefox 57 running Speedometer 2.0, Redis 4.0.2 fragmentation benchmark, Ruby microbenchmark and SPECint 2006, under LD_PRELOAD
claimed_speedup: Memory reduced 16% for Firefox (530 MB vs 632 MB) and 39% for Redis versus jemalloc, with under 1% Speedometer score loss; SPEC400.perlbench peak RSS 564 MB vs 664 MB glibc (15% less) at 3.9% runtime overhead; SPECint geomean memory -2.4%, runtime +0.7%. Not a speed win.
compiler_and_flags: Mesh built with gcc 8 -O3 -flto; SPEC with clang 4.0 -O2; glibc 2.26, jemalloc 3.6.0, gperftools 2.5
hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel i7-5600U, 16 GiB RAM, Linux 4.18, Ubuntu Bionic
tradeoffs: Compacts fragmented heaps by merging virtual pages onto one physical page (meshing) with randomized allocation, no pointer relocation; needs Linux/macOS virtual-memory tricks; Bazel build; extra system calls and copies; randomization gives 10.7% runtime overhead on a Ruby microbenchmark.
caveats: Claim is memory footprint, not speed; the PLDI 2019 numbers use jemalloc 3.6.0 and a 2018 laptop; Hoard and tcmalloc were faster than jemalloc on Speedometer (5.4% and 6.0%) while using more memory.
found_via: Hacker News: threads 'Mesh: Compacting Memory Management for C/C++ Applications' (item 19182779) and 'Mesh: A compacting memory allocator for C/C++' (item 46877714), seen via WebSearch snippets

name: libpas
baseline: bmalloc (WebKit's previous allocator); HN thread also says it beats system malloc in WebKit and JSC
workload: Object churn and memory use inside WebKit; no standalone benchmark data in the repo
claimed_speedup: ReadMe: segregated heaps 'beat the original bmalloc at object churn performance' and use less memory because pages are returned sooner; no numbers on the page
license: BSD-2-Clause (per the Apple copyright header in libpas source files)
stars_or_usage: Ships in Safari/WebKit as bmalloc's backend
tradeoffs: Allocator toolkit built around isoheaps (type-segregated heaps) for security; configurable heap kinds (segregated, bitfit); lives inside the WebKit tree and is built via its own build.sh or CMake; mostly tuned for Apple platforms and WebKit.
caveats: Qualitative claim only, baseline is bmalloc rather than a general-purpose incumbent; the 'beats other mallocs' numbers come from the HN thread 'All About Libpas, Phil's Super Fast Malloc' (item 31581727) and a blocked blog post, seen only as search snippets; last commit date not checked.
found_via: Hacker News: thread 'All About Libpas, Phil's Super Fast Malloc' (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31581727), seen via WebSearch snippets

name: rlsf
workload: Allocation/deallocation latency in cycles on an STM32F401 microcontroller, and WebAssembly code size, for the TLSF constant-time allocator
claimed_speedup: rlsf 260-320 cycles per operation vs dlmalloc 450-750, buddy-alloc 340-440, umm_malloc 300-700; WebAssembly size 1267 bytes vs dlmalloc 9613 bytes and wee_alloc 1910 bytes
tradeoffs: No concurrency (a pool must be locked externally); internal fragmentation proportional to free block size; no special handling of small allocations; no_std; Rust only, not directly callable from C++ without a wrapper.
caveats: Embedded no_std niche: the baselines are embedded allocators, not malloc/jemalloc/mimalloc/Boehm; results are SVG charts with the numbers in alt text; compiler flags not stated; benchmark source not linked from the README.
found_via: Hacker News: thread 'Fast, simple, hard real time allocator for Rust' (item 40220542) and 'Talc' (item 39545574) led to the rlsf repo via WebSearch
